title: LA Creator Sachin Kumar Launches Prema Creative Co. With Indian-American Comedy Series
excerpt: The TikTok creator and aspiring actor has founded a production company dedicated to elevating South Asian voices in Hollywood, debuting with a vertical comedy series called Typecast.
body:
• Sachin Kumar, a Los Angeles-based content creator with over 150,000 TikTok followers, has launched Prema Creative Co. to produce narrative content centering South Asian stories
  • The company's debut project, Typecast, is a vertical comedy series following the experiences of an Indian-American actor navigating Hollywood's casting landscape
  • Kumar built his audience through relatable comedy skits exploring the South Asian-American experience on his sckachi TikTok account
  • The venture reflects a broader shift toward South Asian creators taking ownership of their stories rather than waiting for traditional Hollywood opportunities

Sachin Kumar, a Los Angeles-based content creator and aspiring actor, has launched Prema Creative Co., a production company focused on uplifting South Asian voices through short-form narrative content. The company's first project is Typecast, a vertical comedy series centered on an Indian-American actor trying to make it in Hollywood.

Kumar, who goes by sckachi on TikTok where he has amassed over 150,000 followers, has spent years building an audience with relatable comedy skits that mine the specificities of the South Asian-American experience — from navigating parental expectations to the small cultural collisions of diasporic life. One of his most popular videos, a joke about telling his mom he was going to McDonald's while showing off his passport, has garnered over four million views.

From Skits to Structured Storytelling

With Prema Creative, Kumar is making a deliberate leap from social media comedy to structured storytelling. Typecast draws on the disconnect many South Asian actors face in Hollywood, where roles often reduce them to stereotypes or sideline them entirely. The series follows its protagonist through auditions, callbacks, and the everyday absurdities of pursuing an acting career as a person of color in the entertainment industry.

The vertical format — designed for mobile viewing in the style of platforms like ReelShort and TikTok — positions the series within a rapidly growing segment of the entertainment market. India's own microdrama sector has attracted investment from Jio Hotstar, Yash Raj Films, and Excel Entertainment in recent months, while ReelShort has struck co-production deals across Asia.

Kumar, who studied acting at Michigan State University and has Telugu roots, has been working toward this moment for years. His Backstage profile lists credits spanning theater, film, and television work dating back to his college years, along with training in improvisation, stand-up comedy, and martial arts.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=g_8-SfgUdU0

A Growing Wave of South Asian Creators

Prema Creative arrives at a time when South Asian representation in Hollywood is expanding, though unevenly. While actors like Dev Patel, Mindy Kaling, and Hasan Minhaj have secured prominent roles, the pipeline for emerging South Asian talent remains narrow. Many Indian-American creators have turned to digital platforms to bypass traditional gatekeepers, building audiences on their own terms before leveraging that following into larger projects.

Kumar attended the premiere of Dev Patel's directorial debut Monkey Man, signaling his engagement with the broader South Asian creative community in Los Angeles. His decision to name the company Prema — meaning "love" in several Indian languages — reflects his intent to ground the venture in cultural identity.

"Uplifting South Asian voices through short form, narrative content."

— Prema Creative Co. mission statement

What's Next

Kumar has not announced distribution details for Typecast, though the vertical format suggests it will initially appear on social media platforms or a dedicated streaming channel. The series joins a growing list of indie projects by South Asian-American creators who are choosing to produce content independently rather than wait for traditional industry validation.

For the Indian-American community, the project addresses a persistent gap: comedy that is specifically about the diasporic experience, made by someone living it, rather than filtered through a mainstream Hollywood lens. Whether Prema Creative can scale beyond its first project will depend on audience reception and Kumar's ability to translate his social media following into sustained viewership for longer-form content.
